utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is IT-02-64-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll ask the Prosecution to introduce itself. Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honour. It's Antoinette Issa on behalf of the Prosecution and with me is Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence counsel, could you introduce yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Miodrag Stojanovic. [Interpretation] And today I will be representing Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'd like to welcome all the people present in the courtroom, the representative of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel of the accused, Mr. Borovcanin, and as well as all these people helping us here, the registrar and the usher, as well as the interpreters in their translation booths. As you know, this hearing is dedicated to the status. This is a Status Conference. Let me remind you that the accused was transferred on the 1st of April, 2005, that the initial appearance was held on the 7th of April, 2005, and a new -- there was a new initial appearance on the 5th of May, 2005. As you know, pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Chamber, every four months, every 120 days we need to convene a Status Conference to check that the exchanges between the parties are being carried out in the best possible way and to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial without undue delay. In addition, I will be able to put a number of questions to the accused relating to his state of health and detention conditions. As far as the motions or pending motions are concerned, there is only one, only one currently pending motion, the one which was filed by the Prosecution on the 10th of June, 2005. This is a joinder motion with a view to joining a number of cases. A while ago I held a Status Conference in the presence of Pandurevic and Trbic. I mentioned to them that it would be desirable that the Trial Chamber assigned to render a decision on the joinder motion take a decision shortly, because this does have a bearing on a number of issues, namely the accused whose name I have just mentioned have [sic] been the subject of a preliminary motion regarding a defect in the form of the indictment. This decision will be rendered either by the Trial Chamber that was assigned initially or by the Trial Chamber that would be assigned in the future to render a decision on these motions. And the Pre-Trial Judge who will be handling the case should then be able to prepare his case for the trial in the best conditions possible. It is therefore my duty to check two points out this morning on the disclosure of documents, as you know according it our Rules and pursuant to 66(A)(i) and 66(A)(ii), disclosure of the documents by the Prosecutor to the Defence. I shall now turn to the Prosecutor and ask them where we stand vis-a-vis disclosure of such material. I shall then turn to the Defence counsel. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to Rule 66(A)(i), that has been completed. Counsel has been provided with all such material under that Rule. With respect to Rule 66(A)(ii), the majority of the material that we have has also been provided to counsel. It is presently on the electronic disclosure suite system. Of course, our obligation is ongoing and as new material comes in we are providing that to counsel as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before handing over the floor to the Defence counsel, in the previous Status Conference we addressed the issue of disclosure of documents, and the Prosecution said that the documents had been disclosed electronically. I mentioned that from a personal standpoint I felt it was important for the accused to be provided with the documents, and it is important that the accused be provided with hard-copy documents. If the accused does not have a laptop and does not know how to use one and cannot access the material, then there is an infringement on his rights. It is important that the accused be able to read all the material and all the evidence material against him. I don't know what your point of view is on this, and this is why I shall give you the floor right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It so happens that our Status Conference is the last on the agenda today. I followed the previous Status Conference and also the one in which Ms. Issa took part as well as Mrs. Jelena Nikolic as Defence counsel for Mr. Nikolic. All the issues that were raised earlier in agreement with my colleagues, other Defence counsel, I would just like to repeat and summarise in order not to waste time at this Status Conference. Firstly I would like to confirm Ms. Issa's words. Mr. Borovcanin's Defence counsel has received material pursuant to the Rule 66, and in that respect we don't have any problems. However, I'm going to raise the issue that has been raised already, and this is the case of the cases not having been joined, and we have to deal with a number of Trial Chambers. The first issue is the fact that when we receive material electronically on CD and DVD or in EDS, we can search using Zylab and we can access the relevant parts for our defence, the defence in our case, and it seems to us that this is a very good and efficient solution because we have been able to get rid of a huge binders and papers. However, when we download the relevant elements and when we move them into a particular file, then we no longer can search what is relevant in those documents or parts of those documents, and this is something that is a technical problem at the moment, and we wish to believe that with the help of the registrar we will be able to overcome this problem. However, it seems to me that a second issue at this moment is even more relevant. This second issue is the issue of honouring Rule 66 fully. All of these documents have to be in the language that the accused can understand. In some of the documents we have received so far, we also received transcripts from the Krstic, Blagojevic, and Jokic case. Those transcripts at the moment are not in B/C/S. We can search the documentation and get hold of the relevant parts of these two cases, but none of this is in B/C/S. We have to adjust those transcripts, and we have to go over them in our conversations with the clients whose English does not allow him to use these transcripts. At this stage of the case, we have been allocated certain funds for the interpretation and translation, and I believe that our interpreter will be able to help us with interpreting the relevant parts of the transcript which are in English and thus that we will be able to allow Mr. Borovcanin to understand them and read them before the beginning of trial. Ms. Issa and I have been talking about Srebrenica for a long time now, so at this moment I find it easier than some other colleagues to identify those parts of the supporting material which are important for the defence of Mr. Borovcanin, and in some way this speeds up the procedure for us, especially when we compare ourselves to some other Defence team. The third issue that I would like to raise is the issue that was mentioned at the previous Status Conference. We would like to ask from the OTP to disclose all the material simultaneously to the Defence counsel and to the accused. I'm talking on behalf of Mr. Borovcanin, who has been provided with a PC, who is well-educated and can use the PC or the laptop. I believe that this would speed up the procedure, because if the documents are first disclosed to the Defence counsel and then are discussed with the client and then -- our arrival at The Hague and our conversation with Mr. Borovcanin and given that time is limited may slow down the whole procedure. Another thing that I would like to raise as an issue that you also raised at the former Status Conference is Rule 66 with regard to the disclosure of exculpating material. Before this Trial Chamber we have already discussed the discussion of exculpating material and who is it who should identify the exculpatory material, whether it is the OTP and the Defence, and we agree that this should be the material in its totality and then we would identify what might be exculpatory. Therefore, we don't have any problem receiving all the material from the OTP as it is disclosed and the Defence teams will then be in the position to say what is exculpatory and what is not and it will not expect from the OTP to voice their opinion on that. And finally, I have to say that in our conversation with the Defence team of Mr. Popovic, we were informed that the Presiding Judge in -- has informed the OTP to disclose the list of witnesses that they want to hear as well as the expert reports that they want to present, all the things that they have at the moment. So at the moment we are faced with different practice, and it should be expected from the Trial Chamber to render a decision as soon as possible whether the indictments would be joined so as to enable the Defence teams to know what positions they should take and that in that respect they should have direct communication with the OTP within the context of the defence of their respective clients. I would like to thank you, and I believe that I have only summarised the things that have been mentioned by the four Defence teams. I believe that things are moving very well, that we have very good communication with the OTP, and I, as Defence counsel for Mr. Borovcanin, I don't have any further remarks or objections at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in the light of what you have just said, I have just a few comments to make. You first of all raise an issue which is that of the disclosure by the Prosecution to the accused directly via EDS and via the EDS disclosure system. The counsel has stated that he is not always present in The Hague, and therefore if he cannot discuss with his client these exhibits and -- only when he comes to The Hague, this of course does prejudice the rights of the accused, and therefore the counsel says that in an ideal situation those exhibits should be disclosed to the Defence counsel and to the accused alike given that the accused now has a laptop. Now, as far as this technical problem is concerned, I would like to know what Ms. Issa's position is on this. Personally, I think that it is quite possible to entitle both the Defence counsel and the accused to have the documents disclosed to them at the same time. So what does the Prosecution wish to say on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's position that it's really the obligation of counsel to provide the material to his client. I don't believe the Prosecution has ever been placed in a position even before the EDS system was in place to provide disclosure directly to the accused. Disclosure has always been provided to counsel, and it's just as easy for counsel to send material to his client that he believes the client should be aware of or that he would like to discuss with his client. But it's not the Prosecution's obligation to provide it directly to the accused himself. That would be the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That is your position. Mine is quite a different one. I feel that if a motion is filed, I feel that the accused should be -- have all the documents at hand, notwithstanding the fact that he does have a Defence counsel. That is my position. As the attorney in question has mentioned, he is not always present in The Hague and therefore cannot communicate on a daily basis with his client, in particular when their a whole series of documents to be provided and when there are disclosure issues, the accused may find himself or herself in a position where he cannot have a look at the documents where his counsel can view the documents but not take into account some documents because the accused may have a different viewpoint. I feel that in order to protect the rights of the accused, I think it's very important that the accused be provided with all the documents. I would even take it a step further: I believe that the accused should be provided with hard-copy documents as well. In the facts the accused -- the defendant is accused with, I mentioned that some documents are civil-authority documents or military documents, a number of things that need to be scrutinized either because there are signatures or stamps on these documents, and you cannot answer some of these questions by looking at documents in electronic form. We are currently only in the pre-trial phase. I don't know who is assigned to this case with you rest assured that if I am assigned to this case this is the way I will handle it and I will ask the Prosecution to provide the accused with all the documents. So this is pursuant to Article 66. As regards Rule 66, the Defence counsel raised another issue which has to do with its relation to the Prosecution which I think also affects the right of the accused. In other words, the transcripts of previous trials. The Defence counsel has told us that the transcripts have been made available in English and whilst the accused would like to be able to read them in B/C/S, which is his native language. And if the Prosecution discloses transcripts of previous cases to the Defence, these transcripts need to be in B/C/S, because the accused is entitled to read these transcripts and be familiar with what happened in the course of these trials. What does the Prosecution have to say about this technical matter which touches upon a very essential issue, i.e., that of the rights of the accused? Ms. Issa, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We have provided not only the English transcripts to Mr. Stojanovic, but we've also provided the audio versions of the testimony in -- on DVDs so that he does have the B/C/S version in audio format. It would be -- as Your Honour is aware, and I know Mr. Stojanovic is aware, these transcripts are all of a public nature which Mr. Stojanovic has access to and indeed any counsel has access to. We have provided them as a matter of courtesy to assist counsel. It would not be -- it would be the obligation of registry to transcribe transcripts in the B/C/S language should Mr. Stojanovic want those specific transcripts in the B/C/S language. Having said that, however, he does have the B/C/S transcripts in the audio format, and we've already given that to him so he has access to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Defence counsel, in the light of what you have told us, the Prosecution has just said that you have the audiotapes of these ten trials. Your -- how can your client listen to these audiotapes in English if he only speaks B/C/S? Unless the audiotapes are also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You have been informed that we do have access to audiotapes from the trials which were public, and in that case our client can follow the transcript on audio with the voice in B/C/S and translation in English. So by listening to all these CDs and DVDs, he can listen to the questions and answers which were in B/C/S. This is correct. But it is also correct that this is a very demanding task because this implies a lot of time that the client would need to spend listening to all these tapes. We have already spent over 200 days in the Blagojevic Jokic case, and we have the audiotape from that case. Then you can imagine how much time it would take to listen carefully to all that, because none of this can be curtailed. It is much easier -- it would be much easier to follow all that as a transcript. I would just like to tell you that we will try and overcome this problem by means of a proposal that I have put forth, and that is that we will use our interpreter and the funds that have been allocated to us and that we will end up with a translation in hard copy of those parts that are relevant for the defence of Mr. Borovcanin. I can say that I am familiar with the witnesses that were relevant in those cases, so we will focus on translating those parts of the transcript, and we will provide our client with a hard copy of those relevant parts. However, I assure you that in order to have a fair trial, it would be much more useful to have the audiotape of Krstic, Blagojevic, Jokic case and the translation in hard copy from that case. I'm going to say just one more thing. Most of these witnesses gave interviews to the OTP before the case went into trial, and these interviews do exist in B/C/S version. I personally was in the situation to provide my client with those statements and interviews. Ms. Issa knows it only too well that there were discrepancies between the interviews of these witnesses and their statements during the trial and those discrepancies were sometimes really very relevant. One of those witnesses was an accused who has entered a guilty plea. He changed his statement, and a part of the transcript from his evidence is very relevant for our case, and I believe that in respect of Rule 66 it would be only fair for the Defence that everything should be disclosed in the language that the accused understands. We want to overcome this problem, and I don't think we should become overdramatic at this stage of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Thank you for what you have just mentioned. I think there are a number of small issues that still need to be resolved. I don't know which Trial Chamber will be assigned to this case, but if I were to be assigned as Pre-Trial Judge and handling this case, I would definitely ask the Prosecutor to draw up a list of all the witnesses they intend to call to testify during the trial. I would also like the Prosecution to stipulate which exhibits it intends to use when these witnesses are called to testify. I should also like to ask the Prosecution to complete this list and include the relevant portions of the indictment that relate to these exhibits. It is of course quite certain that the Prosecution will not need all the exhibits it has put on its list, but with a view to having a fair trial and with a view to respecting the rights of the Defence, I think the Prosecution must provide all those exhibits which relate to the witness that will come and testify. These exhibits are the exhibits which will be used during the examination-in-chief. That is just a minimum requirement. If in the course of the examination-in-chief the Prosecutor uses testimonies or statements or testimonies that have been taken in other cases, like in the case of the Blagojevic case, then it goes without saying that those portions which will be quoted must be provided in B/C/S. That, I think, is a minimum requirement which the accused is entitled to. The person who will be handling this case will have to settle this issue, but as far as I'm concerned, that's the way I would do things. The accused must be provided with all the material in his own language, all the material and evidence material which will be used by the Prosecution, which contain all the exhibits and documents and -- documents against the accused. An electronic system is very good, but it is not a perfect system. It might be a little bit too early to address all these issues, but these are real issues and these issues crop up again and again in every trial. So it is important to address try and address these in the pre-trial phase to avoid wasting time in the trial itself discussing matters like a document that hadn't been translated or a document that hasn't been disclosed to the Defence, for instance. We have just mentioned those documents which need to be disclosed pursuant to Rule 66. Under Rule 68, all exculpatory material which may suggest innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused as regards the crimes he is accused of. I shall now turn to Ms. Issa. Have you disclosed to the Defence all the Rule 68 documents or is it that you have not come across any such documents and therefore have not disclosed any to the Defence? You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Rule -- any Rule 68 material would also be -- would have also been placed on the EDS system which counsel has access to. So essentially all material whether it's exculpatory or not is on the EDS system and counsel does have access to all this material. And of course of process is still ongoing, as we are in fairly early stages of these particular proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has just told us that this has been provided to you via EDS. Do you confirm this, Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall now move on to another question which I will put directly to the accused. Could you stand up, please. First question regarding your state of health. Do you have any problems? Is there something you with like to draw my attention on or is everything fine?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your concern. I can inform you that I don't have any health problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as your detention conditions are concerned, do people come and visit you? Are you able to make telephone calls? Are the conditions in detention good or do you have any complaints to file?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already told you, the conditions of my stay and the organisation of life in the Detention Unit is at a very high level. Everything is very professional. I would like to take this opportunity to say that over the past two months I have had a technical problem in communication with my Defence counsel. I have had problems with the privileged telephone line that has been allocated to me. We've had a technical problem. I could not establish communication. However, the -- Mr. McFadden has invested a lot of effort in order to resolve that and this problem was solved yesterday. I have been given a new privileged number. But at this moment I would like to draw your attention to the fact that I did have that problem for two months and I did have some problems in communication with my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that for a period of two months you were unable to contact your lawyer? Did this last two months?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the total duration of this problem. However, at the beginning I did not inform anybody because I thought it was just a temporary thing. Then I spoke with the management of the Detention Unit. I informed them about the problem. They told me that it was a technical problem with the switchboard, and finally this problem was solved with the effort invested by the Detention Unit management.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as your rights are concerned, have you found it in any way difficult to access documents? You have been -- we have been told that you've been provided with a laptop. Are there a number of things which could be improved on, do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very happy with that. I have even more material that I can deal with. However, whatever has been mentioned today, if they constitute an improvement, I am only too glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is there any other issue which you would like to raise or do you feel that all your questions have been answered?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am satisfied everything is in good order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You may sit down. As I have just mentioned, we are all awaiting the decision that will be rendered by the Trial Chamber on the question of the joinder motion. We hope that the decision will be rendered very quickly. A Trial Chamber will then be assigned. A Pre-Trial Judge will be assigned to this Trial Chamber, and it is that Pre-Trial Judge who will then prepare the case. This may raise a number of issues given the number of accused involved, but if things are prepared well in advance and problems are settled well in advance, then the trial can unfold smoothly, and a number of issues will therefore be settled beforehand. Before adjourning the hearing, would anyone like to raise another issue? The Prosecution first and then I shall put the same question to the Defence. Ms. Issa, would you like to raise any other issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence counsel, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, thank you. Just one sentence for the record. Over the past two months my client and I had regular telephone communication, but we did not use the confidential line, the privileged line. We had normal telephone conversations, and I visited my client on two occasions. I hope that the problem was resolved yesterday and that from now on we will continue having privileged communication as we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All the items on the agenda for today have been addressed. So if a decision is rendered and if another Judge is assigned to the Trial Chamber, then you will be talking to someone else. Otherwise, I will have the pleasure of seeing you again. The Court stands adjourned.
